claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy has greater local lattice distortion than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC counterparts.
The quinary alloy has greater atomic-scale chemical fluctuations than the quaternary and ternary counterparts.
Greater lattice distortion and chemical fluctuations enhance dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning increases work hardening.
The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
The quinary alloy has a higher atomic-size mismatch than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary alloy develops larger and more diverse local lattice distortions than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion more effectively in the quinary alloy than in the quaternary or ternary alloys.
More effective impediment of dislocation motion produces increased yield strength in the quinary alloy.
More effective impediment of dislocation motion produces enhanced strain hardening in the quinary alloy.
Relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys, the quinary alloy will exhibit larger and more heterogeneous local strain fields.
Larger and more heterogeneous local strain fields will correlate with higher work hardening.
The quinary alloy will show a delayed onset of plastic instability relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The proposed comparison uses identical thermomechanical processing and room-temperature tensile testing at moderate strain rates.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to identically processed, single-phase FCC alloys.
